P.title: P.blurb
Portugal: History, places, food, music and nature of Portugal, from the Algarve to the Azores.

P.title: wo-portugal.q0.q
Portugal: What is Portugal's only national park?

P.title: wo-portugal.q1.q
Portugal: Which large reservoir is on the Guadiana?

P.title: wo-portugal.q2.q
Portugal: How many islands make up the Azores?

P.title: wo-portugal.c0.text
Portugal: Mainland Portugal is a rectangle about 560 km long and 220 km wide. With the Azores and Madeira, the country covers about 92,000 km² and has around 10.6 million people.

P.title: wo-portugal.c1.text
Portugal: Portugal includes two autonomous regions in the Atlantic: the Azores (nine islands) and Madeira (Madeira, Porto Santo and uninhabited islets).

P.title: wo-portugal.c2.text
Portugal: The north is greener, more mountainous and densely populated near the coast; the south is flatter and drier, with the Alentejo's plains and the Algarve's beaches. The Tejo roughly divides them.

P.title: wo-portugal.c3.text
Portugal: Most people live near the coast between Viana do Castelo and Setúbal. The interior has been losing population for decades, a challenge for services and fire prevention.

P.title: wo-portugal.c4.text
Portugal: Common regions (NUTS II): Norte, Centro, Área Metropolitana de Lisboa, Alentejo and Algarve. Older provinces like Minho, Trás-os-Montes and Beira are still used in everyday speech.

P.title: wo-portugal.c5.text
Portugal: The Minho, in the far northwest, is green and rainy, known for vinho verde, granite villages, the Lima and Minho rivers, and towns like Viana do Castelo, Ponte de Lima and Braga.

P.title: wo-portugal.c5.viz.items.3
Portugal: Ponte de Lima, Portugal's oldest town charter (1125)

P.title: wo-portugal.c6.text
Portugal: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects granite mountains, oak forests, wild Garrano horses, wolves and traditional villages along the Spanish border.

P.title: wo-portugal.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal's big rivers have many dams for hydropower and water storage. The Alqueva reservoir on the Guadiana, completed in 2002, is one of Western Europe's largest artificial lakes.

P.title: wo-portugal.c8.text
Portugal: The Azores lie about 1,400 km west of Lisbon on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. They're volcanic, green and famous for crater lakes, hot springs, whales and tea plantations.

P.title: wo-portugal.c9.text
Portugal: Madeira, about 1,000 km southwest of Lisbon, is a steep volcanic island with laurel forests (UNESCO), levadas (irrigation channels with walking paths) and its famous fortified wine.

P.title: hi-portugal.summary
Portugal: From county to kingdom, and the battle that saved it.

P.title: hi-portugal.q0.q
Portugal: Which city is called "the cradle of Portugal"?

P.title: hi-portugal.q0.x
Portugal: Afonso Henriques' base; São Mamede was nearby.

P.title: hi-portugal.q1.q
Portugal: Who won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385?

P.title: hi-portugal.q2.q
Portugal: What is the Treaty of Windsor (1386)?

P.title: hi-portugal.q2.o1
Portugal: The oldest diplomatic alliance still in force

P.title: hi-portugal.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal began as a county of the kingdom of León, named after Portucale, today's Porto area. In 1096 it was given to Henry of Burgundy and his wife Teresa.

P.title: hi-portugal.c1.text
Portugal: Young Afonso Henriques defeated his mother Teresa's forces at the Battle of São Mamede near Guimarães in 1128, taking control of the county. Guimarães is called "the cradle of Portugal".

P.title: hi-portugal.c2.text
Portugal: At the Treaty of Zamora (1143), Alfonso VII of León recognised Afonso as king. The Pope formally confirmed it in 1179 with the bull Manifestis Probatum.

P.title: hi-portugal.c3.text
Portugal: Afonso and his successors took Santarém and Lisbon (1147), then the Alentejo and finally the Algarve (1249). Portugal's borders, set by the Treaty of Alcañices in 1297, are among Europe's oldest.

P.title: hi-portugal.c4.text
Portugal: Dom Dinis (reigned 1279–1325) planted the pine forest of Leiria to protect farmland and supply timber, founded the university, made Portuguese the official language of documents and created the Order of Christ.

P.title: hi-portugal.c5.text
Portugal: When King Fernando died without a son, Castile claimed the throne. Many Portuguese backed João, Master of Avis. The crisis became a fight for independence.

P.title: hi-portugal.c6.text
Portugal: On 14 August 1385, a smaller Portuguese army under Nuno Álvares Pereira and King João I, with English archers, defeated Castile at Aljubarrota using defensive tactics. Independence was secured.

P.title: hi-portugal.c7.text
Portugal: João I built the Monastery of Santa Maria da Vitória at Batalha to give thanks for Aljubarrota. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site and a masterpiece of Gothic and Manueline art.

P.title: hi-portugal.c8.text
Portugal: The Treaty of Windsor (1386) between Portugal and England is the oldest diplomatic alliance in the world still in force. João I married Philippa of Lancaster, mother of Prince Henry the Navigator.

P.title: hi-portugal.c8.viz.events.2.l
Portugal: João I marries Philippa of Lancaster

P.title: hi-portugal.c9.text
Portugal: The Avis kings launched the overseas expansion: Ceuta (1415), the Atlantic islands, the African coast and finally India. It was the start of Portugal's golden age.

P.title: hi-discovery.title
Portugal: Portugal and the Age of Discovery

P.title: hi-discovery.summary
Portugal: How a small kingdom at the edge of Europe opened the world's sea routes.

P.title: hi-discovery.q0.q
Portugal: What could a caravel do better than a square-rigged ship?

P.title: hi-discovery.q0.o2
Portugal: Sail faster with the wind behind

P.title: hi-discovery.q0.x
Portugal: Its lateen sails let it work into the wind, essential for exploring and getting home.

P.title: hi-discovery.q1.q
Portugal: Who first reached India by sea from Europe?

P.title: hi-discovery.q1.x
Portugal: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

P.title: hi-discovery.q2.o0
Portugal: Cabral claimed it and it lay on Portugal's side of the Tordesillas line

P.title: hi-discovery.q2.x
Portugal: Cabral landed in 1500, and the land fell east of the 1494 treaty line.

P.title: hi-discovery.q3.q
Portugal: Where was Portugal's main base in India?

P.title: hi-discovery.q4.q
Portugal: Who were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543?

P.title: hi-discovery.c0.title
Portugal: Why Portugal turned to the sea

P.title: hi-discovery.c0.text
Portugal: In the 1400s Portugal was small, poor and boxed in by Castile. The rich trade in spices and silk came overland from Asia and was controlled by Venice and Muslim middlemen.\n\nThe Atlantic was the one open door. Prince Henry 'the Navigator' sponsored expeditions down the African coast, step by step, hoping to reach gold, allies and eventually the spices of India by sea.

P.title: hi-discovery.c1.text
Portugal: Square sails work beautifully with the wind behind you, but badly against it. The caravel's triangular 'lateen' sails let it sail much closer into the wind, and its shallow hull could explore coasts and rivers.\n\nThat mattered: coming home from West Africa meant fighting the prevailing winds. Explorers learned to swing far out into the Atlantic to catch better ones.

P.title: hi-discovery.c1.sketch.1
Portugal: triangular sails: closer to the wind

P.title: hi-discovery.c2.text
Portugal: On open water there are no landmarks. In the northern hemisphere, the height of the Pole Star above the horizon roughly equals your latitude. Sailors measured it with a quadrant or astrolabe.\n\nFurther south the Pole Star disappears, so Portuguese navigators measured the Sun at noon instead and used printed tables to correct for the season.

P.title: hi-discovery.c2.sketch.2
Portugal: Lisbon: the Pole Star sits about 39° up

P.title: hi-discovery.c3.text
Portugal: Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488. Ten years later Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India, opening the sea route to the spice trade and making Lisbon one of Europe's richest ports.\n\nIn 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral, heading for India, swung so far west that he reached Brazil. And Fernão de Magalhães (Magellan), a Portuguese sailing for Spain, led the first voyage around the world, completed by Elcano in 1522.

P.title: hi-discovery.c4.text
Portugal: In 1494 Portugal and Castile signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a line from pole to pole 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. New lands to the west would go to Castile, to the east to Portugal.\n\nThe tip of South America that bulged east of the line became Brazil, which is a big part of why around 210 million Brazilians speak Portuguese today.

P.title: hi-discovery.c5.text
Portugal: Infante D. Henrique (1394–1460) didn't sail far himself, but he organised and funded voyages down the African coast from the Algarve, gathering pilots, mapmakers and shipbuilders.

P.title: hi-discovery.c6.text
Portugal: Pepper, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg were worth fortunes in Europe. The sea route to India let Portugal buy at the source, bypassing Venetian and Middle Eastern middlemen.

P.title: hi-discovery.c6.viz.steps.0
Portugal: Spices in India and the Moluccas

P.title: hi-discovery.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal built a network of trading posts and forts: Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz and later Macau (1557). Portuguese traders were the first Europeans to reach Japan, in 1543.

P.title: hi-discovery.c8.text
Portugal: The voyages also opened the Atlantic slave trade. Over three and a half centuries, Portuguese and Brazilian ships carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other nation's, a history now studied and acknowledged.

P.title: hi-discovery.c8.viz.items.3
Portugal: Abolished in Portugal's empire in stages in the 1800s

P.title: hi-discovery.c9.text
Portugal: The voyages connected continents, spread crops (maize, potatoes, tomatoes to Europe; sugar, coffee to the Americas), languages and diseases, and began globalisation, with both benefits and great suffering.

P.title: pt-lisbon.summary
Portugal: Hills, trams, river light and nearly 3,000 years of history in Portugal's capital.

P.title: pt-lisbon.q0.q
Portugal: Where does the name Alfama probably come from?

P.title: pt-lisbon.q0.x
Portugal: A trace of the Moorish city.

P.title: pt-lisbon.q1.q
Portugal: Which two Belém monuments are UNESCO World Heritage?

P.title: pt-lisbon.q2.q
Portugal: When did the 25 de Abril Bridge open?

P.title: pt-lisbon.q2.x
Portugal: As the Salazar Bridge, renamed after 1974.

P.title: pt-lisbon.q3.q
Portugal: Who designed the Santa Justa lift?

P.title: pt-lisbon.q3.x
Portugal: A Porto-born engineer of French parents.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c0.text
Portugal: Lisbon climbs a set of steep hills on the north bank of the Tagus, just before the river meets the Atlantic. Tradition says there are seven, like Rome.\n\nIt is one of Europe's oldest cities and has been Portugal's capital since the 13th century. The city itself is small, but greater Lisbon holds over a quarter of the country's people.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c1.text
Portugal: Alfama, below the castle, is Lisbon's oldest quarter. Its name comes from Arabic, and its maze of steep alleys, stairways and tiny squares still follows the shape of the Moorish town.\n\nMuch of it survived the 1755 earthquake. Today it is a heartland of Lisbon fado and of the June festivals.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c2.text
Portugal: Belém, on the river west of the centre, is where fleets left for Africa, India and Brazil. Its monuments celebrate that age of voyages.\n\nThe Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower, both in the ornate Manueline style, have been UNESCO World Heritage since 1983.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c3.text
Portugal: In the 1500s Lisbon was one of the busiest ports in Europe. Pepper, silk and porcelain from Asia, sugar from Brazil and gold from Africa passed along its riverside.\n\nIt was a crowded, cosmopolitan city, with merchants from all over Europe and a large African population, many of them enslaved.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c4.text
Portugal: The 1755 earthquake, tsunami and fire destroyed the lower town. It was rebuilt as the Baixa, a grid of straight streets running from the river to Rossio.\n\nToday you can walk the whole plan in about fifteen minutes, from the riverside square, under a triumphal arch, to the old city squares.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c5.text
Portugal: Lisbon's hills made getting around hard, so the city built funiculars, a street lift and a tram network. The small yellow trams, like the famous number 28, still rattle through the old quarters.\n\nUnderground runs the Metro, opened in 1959, with four lines and many stations decorated with azulejos.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c6.text
Portugal: Lisbon's hills give it dozens of miradouros: public viewpoints with benches, kiosks and views over red roofs to the river.\n\nThe city is also famous for its light. Strong sun, reflected off the wide Tagus and pale limestone pavements, gives it a bright, golden glow.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c7.text
Portugal: For centuries, crossing the Tagus at Lisbon meant taking a boat. In 1966 a great red suspension bridge opened, today called the 25 de Abril. In 1998 the Vasco da Gama Bridge followed, one of the longest in Europe.\n\nFerries still cross too, linking Lisbon with Cacilhas, Seixal and Barreiro.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c8.text
Portugal: Expo 98 transformed about 5 km of Lisbon's eastern waterfront, an area of oil depots, warehouses and a slaughterhouse.\n\nAfter the fair closed, the site became Parque das Nações, a new district of homes, offices and gardens with some of Portugal's best-known modern architecture.

P.title: pt-lisbon.c9.text
Portugal: Since the 2010s Lisbon has become one of Europe's most visited cities and a hub for start-ups. Old buildings have been restored and the centre buzzes with visitors.\n\nThe boom has a cost: rents and house prices have risen far faster than wages, pushing many residents out of the historic quarters.

P.title: pt-porto.summary
Portugal: The city that named a country and a wine, and the green granite north around it.

P.title: pt-porto.q0.q
Portugal: Who designed the Dom Luís I Bridge?

P.title: pt-porto.q0.x
Portugal: Eiffel's former partner; Eiffel's firm built the Maria Pia.

P.title: pt-porto.q1.q
Portugal: How does port wine keep its sweetness?

P.title: pt-porto.q1.x
Portugal: The yeast stops before all the sugar is used.

P.title: pt-porto.q2.q
Portugal: What were rabelo boats used for?

P.title: pt-porto.q2.o1
Portugal: Carrying port wine down the Douro

P.title: pt-porto.q2.x
Portugal: Pipes of wine went from the farms to Gaia.

P.title: pt-porto.q3.o1
Portugal: It held out through the 1832–33 siege

P.title: pt-porto.c0.text
Portugal: Porto grew on a granite hill above the Douro, near the river's mouth. Its Roman port, Portus Cale, gave its name to Portugal.\n\nA proud merchant city, it is nicknamed "Invicta", the unconquered, and its people are "tripeiros", tripe-eaters, after a story from 1415.

P.title: pt-porto.c1.text
Portugal: The Ribeira is Porto's old riverside quarter: tall, narrow houses in bright colours stacked up the slope above the Douro quay.\n\nTogether with the old centre and the Dom Luís I Bridge, it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

P.title: pt-porto.c2.text
Portugal: Six bridges cross the Douro between Porto and Gaia. The iron Maria Pia railway bridge (1877) was built by Gustave Eiffel's company.\n\nThe Dom Luís I Bridge (1886) has two decks: the upper one now carries the Metro, the lower one cars and walkers beside the Ribeira.

P.title: pt-porto.c3.text
Portugal: Port is a fortified wine from the Douro. Adding grape spirit part-way through fermentation stops the yeast, leaving natural sweetness and about 20% alcohol.\n\nFor centuries the wine was shipped down the river and aged in the lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto, before export.

P.title: pt-porto.c4.text
Portugal: Upstream from Porto, the Douro cuts through steep schist hills that people have carved into terraces of vines over centuries.\n\nThe Alto Douro Wine Region, one of the oldest demarcated wine regions in the world, has been a UNESCO cultural landscape since 2001.

P.title: pt-porto.c5.text
Portugal: For centuries, port wine travelled from the Douro farms to Gaia in rabelos: flat-bottomed wooden boats with a square sail and a long steering oar.\n\nRailways, roads and dams ended the trade, but rabelos still float by the Gaia lodges and race on São João's day.

P.title: pt-porto.c6.text
Portugal: Two old cities of the Minho sit about 25 km apart. Braga, founded by the Romans, has been a religious capital for over 1,500 years and is crowded with churches.\n\nGuimarães, linked to Portugal's first king, has a beautifully kept medieval centre listed by UNESCO.

P.title: pt-porto.c7.text
Portugal: The north-west of Portugal is built of granite and soaked by Atlantic rain. Walls, houses, churches and even vine posts are made of it.\n\nMild, wet weather keeps the Minho green all year, with small fields, woods and fast rivers flowing down from the mountains.

P.title: pt-porto.c8.text
Portugal: The North is Portugal's manufacturing heartland. Thousands of family firms make textiles, clothing, shoes, furniture and cork products, much of it for export.\n\nAfter hard years of competition from Asia, many moved upmarket, selling design, speed and quality rather than low prices.

P.title: pt-porto.c9.text
Portugal: Porto has reinvented itself since the 2000s, with landmark architecture, a light-rail Metro, a booming tourist trade and lively universities.\n\nIt is also Portugal's architecture capital: Álvaro Siza and Eduardo Souto de Moura, both Pritzker Prize winners, come from the Porto school.

P.title: pt-islands.summary
Portugal: Volcanic islands in the Atlantic: how they formed, who settled them and how they live today.

P.title: pt-islands.q0.o1
Portugal: A hotspot under the African plate

P.title: pt-islands.q0.o2
Portugal: A piece of Africa that broke off

P.title: pt-islands.q0.x
Portugal: The plate slides slowly over a hot column of mantle.

P.title: pt-islands.q1.q
Portugal: Which eruption of 1957–58 led to emigration to the USA?

P.title: pt-islands.q1.x
Portugal: The US passed the Azorean Refugee Act in 1958.

P.title: pt-islands.q2.q
Portugal: When was the last sperm whale hunted in the Azores?

P.title: pt-islands.q3.o2
Portugal: It is aged under the sea

P.title: pt-islands.c0.text
Portugal: Both archipelagos are the tops of huge volcanoes that rise thousands of metres from the Atlantic floor.\n\nThe Azores sit where three tectonic plates meet, near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Madeira lies in the middle of the African plate, above a hotspot of hot, rising mantle rock.

P.title: pt-islands.c1.text
Portugal: The Azores are still geologically active. Earthquakes are frequent, and several volcanoes have erupted since settlement, both on land and under the sea.\n\nThe 1957–58 Capelinhos eruption on Faial added new land to the island and led thousands of islanders to emigrate to the United States.

P.title: pt-islands.c2.text
Portugal: Unlike the Canary Islands, Madeira and the Azores had no native people when Portuguese sailors arrived in the early 1400s.\n\nSettlers came from mainland Portugal and, on some Azorean islands, from Flanders. They cleared forest, brought animals and crops, and built new societies from scratch.

P.title: pt-islands.c3.text
Portugal: The islands' economies have changed again and again. Madeira had a sugar boom in the late 1400s, then turned to wine. The Azores grew wheat and dye plants, then exported oranges to Britain.\n\nToday dairy farming dominates the Azores, while tourism leads in Madeira.

P.title: pt-islands.c4.text
Portugal: The ocean keeps both archipelagos mild all year. Madeira is subtropical, with warm winters on its sunny south coast. The Azores are cooler, wetter and windier, with changeable skies.\n\nThe mountains create big contrasts: wet, cloudy north slopes and drier south coasts.

P.title: pt-islands.c5.text
Portugal: Madeira's laurel forest is a famous survivor, but laurisilva once covered much of the Azores too. There, most was cut down for fields and pasture, and invasive plants now threaten the rest.\n\nProtecting these forests also protects rare island birds such as the priolo of São Miguel.

P.title: pt-islands.c6.text
Portugal: For about a century, Azorean men hunted sperm whales from small open boats with hand-thrown harpoons. The last one was killed in 1987.\n\nTwo years later the first whale-watching company started on Pico. Today whale-watching is a major part of the islands' tourism.

P.title: pt-islands.c7.text
Portugal: Since 1976 the Azores and Madeira have been autonomous regions, with their own elected parliaments and governments that run most local affairs.\n\nThey are also "outermost regions" of the European Union, which allows special support and rules because of their distance and small island economies.

P.title: pt-islands.c8.text
Portugal: Madeira wine is fortified like port, but then deliberately warmed for months or years. This "cooking" gives it nutty, caramel flavours and makes it almost indestructible.\n\nFour classic grapes give four styles, from dry Sercial to rich, sweet Malvasia, also called Malmsey.

P.title: pt-islands.c9.text
Portugal: For centuries, island life meant emigration. Azoreans went to Brazil, then to New England, California and Canada. Madeirans went to Venezuela, South Africa, Brazil and the UK.\n\nEmigrant communities keep close ties with home, while tourism, cheaper flights and remote work now bring new people to the islands.

P.title: pt-language.summary
Portugal: From the Latin of Gallaecia to a global language of about 260 million speakers.

P.title: pt-language.q0.x
Portugal: Latin cl- at the start of a word turned into ch-.

P.title: pt-language.q1.q
Portugal: Which language gave Portuguese aldeia, açúcar and almofada?

P.title: pt-language.q1.x
Portugal: Centuries of Muslim rule left hundreds of Arabic words, many starting with al- or a-.

P.title: pt-language.q2.q
Portugal: In which language did medieval poets across Iberia write their love songs?

P.title: pt-language.q2.x
Portugal: Even Alfonso X of Castile wrote his Marian songs in it.

P.title: pt-language.q3.q
Portugal: What does Portugal's "estou a ler" usually become in Brazil?

P.title: pt-language.q3.x
Portugal: Brazil uses the gerund for ongoing actions.

P.title: pt-language.q4.q
Portugal: What did the 1990 agreement change in Portugal's spelling?

P.title: pt-language.q4.o1
Portugal: It dropped many silent consonants, as in ação

P.title: pt-language.q4.o2
Portugal: It made every spelling identical to Brazil's

P.title: pt-language.q4.x
Portugal: Acção became ação and óptimo became ótimo.

P.title: pt-language.c0.text
Portugal: Portuguese is a Romance language: it grew out of the everyday Latin spoken in the Roman west of Iberia.\n\nOver many centuries that Latin changed sound by sound until it became a new language. Most Portuguese words still go back to Latin, even when they look very different today.

P.title: pt-language.c1.text
Portugal: In the Middle Ages, people on both banks of the Minho spoke one language, now called Galician-Portuguese.\n\nWhen Portugal became an independent kingdom and expanded south, its speech drifted away from that of Galicia, which came under Castile. Galician and Portuguese are still very close relatives.

P.title: pt-language.c2.text
Portugal: From 711, much of Iberia was ruled by Muslim states; in what is now southern Portugal, until 1249.\n\nArabic was the language of learning, farming and trade, and Portuguese absorbed several hundred of its words, from the kitchen to the building site, plus place names all over the south.

P.title: pt-language.c3.text
Portugal: In the 13th and 14th centuries, Galician-Portuguese was the fashionable language of lyric poetry across Christian Iberia.\n\nKings, nobles and wandering jograis composed songs of love, longing and mockery. About 1,700 of these cantigas survive, copied into a handful of medieval songbooks.

P.title: pt-language.c3.viz.items.0
Portugal: Cantigas de amigo: a girl's voice

P.title: pt-language.c3.viz.items.1
Portugal: Cantigas de amor: a man's lament

P.title: pt-language.c4.text
Portugal: Luís Vaz de Camões gave Portuguese its great epic. Os Lusíadas, printed in 1572, retells Vasco da Gama's voyage to India as the story of a whole people.\n\nIts success helped fix Portuguese as a literary language, which is still often called "the language of Camões".

P.title: pt-language.c5.text
Portugal: From the 1400s, Portuguese sailors, traders and missionaries carried their language along the coasts of Africa, Asia and South America.\n\nFor about two centuries it served as a common trading language in many ports. It left behind new creole languages and a trail of borrowed words.

P.title: pt-language.c6.text
Portugal: Portuguese has about 260 million speakers, which puts it among the ten most spoken languages on Earth.\n\nAbout eight in ten live in Brazil. Portugal itself has only around 4% of the world's speakers, and Africa's share is the one growing fastest.

P.title: pt-language.c7.text
Portugal: European and Brazilian Portuguese are one language with two standards, a little like British and American English.\n\nThey differ in pronunciation, some grammar, vocabulary and the everyday word for "you". Speakers understand each other well, with the occasional laugh over false friends.

P.title: pt-language.c8.text
Portugal: For most of the 20th century, Portugal and Brazil spelled many words differently.\n\nThe Orthographic Agreement, signed in Lisbon in 1990, set common rules for all Portuguese-speaking countries. It took decades to apply and is still debated, but schools and official texts in Portugal and Brazil now follow it.

P.title: pt-language.c9.text
Portugal: European Portuguese sounds softer and more compact than its spelling suggests; some foreigners even mistake it for a Slavic language.\n\nLearners struggle with nasal vowels, unstressed vowels that almost vanish and a final s that sounds like "sh". The letter x alone has four different sounds.

P.title: pt-lusophone.summary
Portugal: The CPLP, nine countries, old outposts in Asia and the Portuguese diaspora.

P.title: pt-lusophone.q0.x
Portugal: The Community was founded in Lisbon in 1996.

P.title: pt-lusophone.q1.q
Portugal: Which country joined the CPLP in 2014 after making Portuguese an official language?

P.title: pt-lusophone.q1.x
Portugal: A former Spanish colony with a Portuguese past on Annobón.

P.title: pt-lusophone.q2.q
Portugal: Which Portuguese-speaking country is a member of the Commonwealth?

P.title: pt-lusophone.q3.q
Portugal: What are Timor-Leste's two official languages?

P.title: pt-lusophone.q3.x
Portugal: Tetum is the main everyday language.

P.title: pt-lusophone.q4.q
Portugal: Which US state is home to the Portuguese communities of Fall River and New Bedford?

P.title: pt-lusophone.q4.x
Portugal: Azorean whalers settled there in the 1800s.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c0.text
Portugal: The Community of Portuguese Language Countries, the CPLP, was founded in Lisbon in 1996. It now has nine members on four continents, home to about 300 million people.\n\nIt promotes the language, cooperation and easier movement between members, but it has no common market or army.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c1.text
Portugal: Brazil is by far the largest Portuguese-speaking country, with about 213 million people.\n\nA Portuguese colony from 1500, it became independent in 1822 under a Portuguese prince. Today the ties run both ways: Brazilians are now the largest foreign community in Portugal.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c2.text
Portugal: Angola, on Africa's south-west coast, is the second-largest Portuguese-speaking country by population, with about 37 million people.\n\nRich in oil and diamonds, it has rebuilt since a long civil war ended in 2002. Portuguese is spreading fast and is now the first language of many young Angolans.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c3.text
Portugal: Mozambique stretches along Africa's south-east coast on the Indian Ocean, with about 34 million people.\n\nPortuguese is the official language and a bridge between dozens of local languages, though only a minority speak it at home. It was also the first member of the Commonwealth that had never been a British colony.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c4.text
Portugal: Cape Verde is an archipelago of ten volcanic islands about 600 km off West Africa. It was uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived around 1460 and became a crossroads of the Atlantic.\n\nPeople speak Kriolu at home and Portuguese at school, and more Cape Verdeans live abroad than on the islands.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c5.text
Portugal: Guinea-Bissau, on the West African mainland, won independence after an armed struggle led by Amílcar Cabral's movement.\n\nSão Tomé and Príncipe, two small islands in the Gulf of Guinea, was once among the world's leading cocoa producers. In both countries, a Portuguese-based creole is the everyday language for many people.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c6.text
Portugal: Timor-Leste, the eastern half of the island of Timor, was Portuguese for about four centuries.\n\nAfter 24 years of Indonesian occupation, its people voted for independence in 1999, and it became a state in 2002. Portuguese and Tetum are its official languages.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c7.text
Portugal: Macau, on China's south coast, was Portuguese for over 400 years until 1999, and Goa in India for over 450 years until 1961.\n\nFew people there speak Portuguese today, but its legacy lives on in churches, street names, food, family names and law.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c8.text
Portugal: About two million people born in Portugal live abroad, one of the highest shares of any European country.\n\nMost are in Europe, above all in France, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Luxembourg. Their children, the lusodescendentes, often keep the language and close ties to their parents' villages.

P.title: pt-lusophone.c9.text
Portugal: Across the Atlantic, Portuguese communities grew in Brazil, the United States, Canada and Venezuela, many of them from the Azores and Madeira.\n\nAbout 1.3 million Americans and some 450,000 Canadians report Portuguese ancestry, from New England fishing towns to Toronto.

P.title: hi-pt20.summary
Portugal: Dictatorship, colonial wars, revolution and Europe.

P.title: hi-pt20.q0.q
Portugal: What signalled the start of the 25 April 1974 revolution on the radio?

P.title: hi-pt20.q1.q
Portugal: When did Portugal join the European Economic Community?

P.title: hi-pt20.c0.text
Portugal: Salazar's regime rested on "God, Fatherland, Family". It censored the press, banned parties and strikes, used the political police PIDE, and kept Portugal poor and largely rural, with high emigration.

P.title: hi-pt20.c1.text
Portugal: From the 1950s to the 1970s, well over a million Portuguese emigrated, many illegally ("a salto") to France, Germany and Luxembourg, escaping poverty and military service.

P.title: hi-pt20.c2.text
Portugal: From 1961 Portugal fought independence movements in Angola, Guinea-Bissau and Mozambique. Over 13 years, about 800,000 Portuguese men served; around 9,000 died, along with many more Africans.

P.title: hi-pt20.c3.text
Portugal: In the 1958 presidential election, General Humberto Delgado challenged the regime. Asked what he'd do with Salazar, he said: "Obviamente, demito-o!" He lost a fraudulent vote and was murdered by the PIDE in 1965.

P.title: hi-pt20.c3.viz.events.2.l
Portugal: murdered by the PIDE in Spain

P.title: hi-pt20.c4.text
Portugal: Salazar was incapacitated in 1968 after a fall and replaced by Marcelo Caetano, who promised reforms but kept the colonial wars and the regime's core.

P.title: hi-pt20.c5.text
Portugal: On 25 April 1974, young officers of the Armed Forces Movement (MFA) overthrew the regime almost without bloodshed. Crowds filled the streets and put carnations in soldiers' rifles: the Carnation Revolution.

P.title: hi-pt20.c5.viz.events.0.l
Portugal: Grândola, Vila Morena on the radio signals go

P.title: hi-pt20.c5.viz.events.2.l
Portugal: Caetano surrenders at Largo do Carmo

P.title: hi-pt20.c6.text
Portugal: After the revolution, Portugal recognised the independence of Guinea-Bissau (1974), Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Angola (1975). Around half a million "retornados" came to Portugal.

P.title: hi-pt20.c6.viz.events.1.l
Portugal: Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Angola

P.title: hi-pt20.c7.text
Portugal: After a turbulent period (PREC), the 1976 constitution established a democratic republic. Free elections, a free press and local democracy took root.

P.title: hi-pt20.c8.text
Portugal: Portugal joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1986 together with Spain. EU funds helped build roads, schools and hospitals; Portugal adopted the euro in 1999 (coins and notes in 2002).

P.title: hi-pt20.c9.text
Portugal: Expo '98 in Lisbon transformed the eastern waterfront and showcased a modern country. Since then Portugal has faced crises (2011 bailout) and become a major tourism and tech destination.

P.title: pt-democracy.summary
Portugal: The Constitution, President, parliament, government, courts, regions and local power.

P.title: pt-democracy.q0.q
Portugal: How many seats does the Assembly of the Republic have?

P.title: pt-democracy.q1.q
Portugal: For how long is the President of the Republic elected?

P.title: pt-democracy.q1.x
Portugal: Up to two consecutive five-year terms.

P.title: pt-democracy.q2.q
Portugal: Under the d'Hondt method, each list's votes are divided by what?

P.title: pt-democracy.q2.x
Portugal: The largest quotients win the seats.

P.title: pt-democracy.q3.q
Portugal: Who decides whether a law respects the Constitution?

P.title: pt-democracy.q3.x
Portugal: Its 13 judges serve a single nine-year term.

P.title: pt-democracy.q4.q
Portugal: Which two regions have their own parliaments and governments?

P.title: pt-democracy.q4.x
Portugal: They have been autonomous regions since 1976.

P.title: pt-democracy.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal's Constitution was approved on 2 April 1976 by an assembly elected a year after the revolution.\n\nIt defines Portugal as a democratic republic based on human dignity, the rule of law and the separation of powers. It has been revised seven times and remains the supreme law.

P.title: pt-democracy.c1.text
Portugal: The President of the Republic is head of state, elected directly by the people for five years and limited to two consecutive terms.\n\nThe role is mostly that of a referee. The President does not run the government but appoints the Prime Minister, can veto laws and can dissolve parliament.

P.title: pt-democracy.c1.viz.items.1
Portugal: At most two terms in a row

P.title: pt-democracy.c2.text
Portugal: The Assembly of the Republic is Portugal's parliament, a single chamber of 230 members elected for four years.\n\nIt makes laws, approves the budget, can bring down the government and elects key officials. It meets in the São Bento Palace in Lisbon, a former Benedictine monastery.

P.title: pt-democracy.c3.text
Portugal: Seats are shared out by proportional representation: parties win seats roughly in line with their votes.\n\nPortugal uses the d'Hondt method, devised by the Belgian lawyer Victor d'Hondt in 1878. In each constituency, voters choose a party list, not individual candidates.

P.title: pt-democracy.c3.example.1
Portugal: Largest quotients: A 10,000, B 8,000, A 5,000, B 4,000, A 3,333

P.title: pt-democracy.c3.example.2
Portugal: A wins 3 seats, B 2, C none

P.title: pt-democracy.c3.viz.items.1.m
Portugal: seats it has won so far

P.title: pt-democracy.c4.text
Portugal: The Government runs the country day to day: it proposes the budget, directs the civil service and can issue decree-laws.\n\nIt is led by the Prime Minister, appointed by the President in light of the election results. A government survives only as long as parliament does not reject or censure it.

P.title: pt-democracy.c5.text
Portugal: The Constitutional Court decides whether laws respect the Constitution and can strike them down. Created by the 1982 revision, it has 13 judges serving a single nine-year term.\n\nAlongside it, independent courts, prosecutors, an Ombudsman and a Court of Auditors keep watch on the other powers.

P.title: pt-democracy.c6.text
Portugal: The Azores and Madeira are autonomous regions, a status the 1976 Constitution created because of their distance from Lisbon and their island identity.\n\nEach has its own elected assembly and regional government, which make laws on many local matters. Defence, foreign policy and justice stay with the national state.

P.title: pt-democracy.c7.text
Portugal: Local government has two levels: 308 municipalities, the concelhos, and below them more than 3,000 parishes, the freguesias.\n\nEach has elected bodies that run local services such as roads, schools, water, waste and culture. Mayors and parish presidents are often the politicians people know best.

P.title: pt-democracy.c8.text
Portugal: Citizens aged 18 and over vote in national, presidential, local, regional and European elections, and in occasional referendums.\n\nElections are held on Sundays, overseen by an independent commission, and votes are counted in public at each polling station.

P.title: pt-democracy.c9.text
Portugal: Since 1986 Portugal has been a member of the European Union, sharing some decisions with 26 other countries.\n\nIt elects 21 members of the European Parliament, sends ministers to the Council and nominates one commissioner. Where the treaties give the EU power, EU law takes priority over national law.

P.title: pt-economy.summary
Portugal: From EU entry and the bailout to tourism, exports, renewables, start-ups and wages.

P.title: pt-economy.q0.q
Portugal: Which country is Portugal's largest export customer?

P.title: pt-economy.q0.x
Portugal: Spain takes around a quarter of Portugal's goods exports.

P.title: pt-economy.q1.q
Portugal: Portugal is the world's largest producer and exporter of which material?

P.title: pt-economy.q1.x
Portugal: Most of it becomes wine stoppers.

P.title: pt-economy.q2.q
Portugal: When did Portugal close its last coal power station?

P.title: pt-economy.q2.x
Portugal: The Pego plant shut in November 2021.

P.title: pt-economy.q3.q
Portugal: How many wage payments do most Portuguese workers receive a year?

P.title: pt-economy.q3.x
Portugal: Twelve months plus holiday and Christmas allowances.

P.title: pt-economy.q4.q
Portugal: Which big tech conference has been held in Lisbon since 2016?

P.title: pt-economy.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal's economy produces about €285 billion of goods and services a year, under 2% of the EU total. Services such as tourism, trade and finance dominate.\n\nExports now equal close to half of GDP, far more than in the past, so the country depends heavily on selling abroad.

P.title: pt-economy.c1.title
Portugal: From EU entry to the euro

P.title: pt-economy.c1.text
Portugal: Joining the European Community in 1986 opened markets and brought large EU funds, and Portugal grew fast for about 15 years.\n\nAfter the euro arrived in 1999, growth slowed sharply. The 2000s became a "lost decade" in which the economy barely grew while debts piled up.

P.title: pt-economy.c2.text
Portugal: In 2011, unable to borrow on the markets at affordable rates, Portugal asked the EU and the IMF for a rescue loan. Three years of spending cuts, tax rises and reforms followed.\n\nThe economy has since recovered: unemployment fell, the state ran budget surpluses in several years and public debt dropped below 100% of GDP.

P.title: pt-economy.c3.text
Portugal: Tourism is one of Portugal's biggest industries. Visitors come for beaches, cities, food, golf and history, and in 2024 tourist lodgings recorded about 31 million guests.\n\nSpending by foreign visitors, about €27 billion a year, makes tourism the country's largest single export.

P.title: pt-economy.c4.text
Portugal: Portugal's goods exports are more varied than many people think. Cars and components lead, followed by machinery, refined fuels, plastics, paper, textiles and shoes.\n\nMost go to other EU countries, above all Spain, as Portuguese firms plug into European supply chains.

P.title: pt-economy.c5.text
Portugal: Portugal is the world's largest producer and exporter of cork, selling about €1.2 billion of it abroad each year.\n\nMost becomes wine stoppers, but cork also goes into floors, insulation, shoes and even spacecraft. Nothing is wasted: offcuts are ground into granules and pressed into new products.

P.title: pt-economy.c6.text
Portugal: Portugal makes around 7 million hectolitres of wine a year, among the world's top dozen producers, and exports close to €1 billion of it.\n\nPort is still the best-known product, but table wines now earn more abroad in total. The industry's aim is to sell fewer cheap bulk wines and more bottles at higher prices.

P.title: pt-economy.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal is one of Europe's leaders in clean electricity. In 2024 renewables, mainly hydro, wind and solar, supplied around 70% of the electricity the country used.\n\nIts last coal power station closed in 2021, and governments have set targets to go higher still by 2030.

P.title: pt-economy.c8.text
Portugal: Since the mid-2010s, Lisbon and Porto have become popular bases for tech start-ups and remote workers.\n\nThe Web Summit, one of the world's largest tech conferences, has been held in Lisbon every November since 2016. A handful of companies with Portuguese founders have grown into "unicorns" valued at over $1 billion.

P.title: pt-economy.c9.text
Portugal: Wages in Portugal are among the lower ones in Western Europe. The national minimum wage has risen quickly, to €920 a month in 2026, paid 14 times a year.\n\nThe deeper issue is productivity: each hour worked produces much less value than the EU average, which limits how far pay can rise.

P.title: pt-sea.summary
Portugal: A small country with a vast ocean: fish, waves, science, energy and a changing coast.

P.title: pt-sea.q0.q
Portugal: About how large is Portugal's exclusive economic zone?

P.title: pt-sea.q1.q
Portugal: Why is the sea on Portugal's west coast cold in summer?

P.title: pt-sea.q1.x
Portugal: North winds push surface water offshore.

P.title: pt-sea.q2.q
Portugal: What makes Nazaré's waves so big?

P.title: pt-sea.q2.x
Portugal: The canyon focuses the energy of the swell.

P.title: pt-sea.q3.q
Portugal: Why does Portugal use floating offshore wind turbines?

P.title: pt-sea.q3.o1
Portugal: The seabed gets deep close to shore

P.title: pt-sea.q3.x
Portugal: Fixed foundations only suit shallow water.

P.title: pt-sea.c0.title
Portugal: A small country, a huge sea

P.title: pt-sea.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal's exclusive economic zone (EEZ), the sea where it controls fishing, energy and seabed resources, covers about 1.7 million km². That is roughly 18 times its land area and one of the largest in Europe.\n\nThe waters around the Azores make up more than half of it.

P.title: pt-sea.c1.text
Portugal: Beyond 200 nautical miles, a country can claim rights to the seabed if it proves the seabed is a natural extension of its land. Portugal submitted such a claim to the United Nations in 2009.\n\nIf accepted, it would add about 2 million km² of seabed, bringing the total to around 4 million km².

P.title: pt-sea.c2.text
Portugal: Swimmers on Portugal's west coast know the Atlantic is cold even in August. The reason is upwelling: summer north winds push surface water away from the coast, and cold, deep water rises to replace it.\n\nThat deep water is full of nutrients, which is why these seas are so rich in fish.

P.title: pt-sea.c3.text
Portugal: The Portuguese eat more fish and seafood per person than anyone else in the EU, about 57 kg a year, more than twice the EU average.\n\nGrilled sardines, octopus, horse mackerel and clams are everyday food, landed by a fleet made up mostly of small boats.

P.title: pt-sea.c4.text
Portugal: Cod doesn't live in Portuguese waters, yet bacalhau is the national dish. For centuries, Portuguese ships sailed to Newfoundland and Greenland to catch it and salt it.\n\nToday most cod comes from Norway and Iceland, and it is still eaten salted, soaked and cooked in hundreds of ways.

P.title: pt-sea.c5.text
Portugal: Nazaré's Praia do Norte produces some of the biggest surfable waves on Earth, over 20 m on the best winter days.\n\nThe secret lies underwater: the Nazaré Canyon, a gorge in the seabed up to about 5,000 m deep, runs almost to the beach and focuses the energy of Atlantic swells.

P.title: pt-sea.c5.viz.steps.2
Portugal: Waves meet at Praia do Norte

P.title: pt-sea.c6.text
Portugal: Portugal's huge sea makes it an important place for ocean research. Hot springs on the seabed near the Azores, deep canyons and seamounts host life found nowhere else.\n\nIn 2024 the Azores created the largest network of marine protected areas in the North Atlantic, covering 30% of its sea.

P.title: pt-sea.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal sits beside some of the world's busiest shipping lanes, between Europe, Africa and the Americas. Its largest port, Sines, is a deep-water hub for container ships and energy.\n\nUnder the sea run fibre-optic cables linking Europe with Africa and the Americas, several of them landing on the Portuguese coast.

P.title: pt-sea.c8.text
Portugal: Portugal's continental shelf is narrow, so the seabed drops steeply away from the coast. That rules out ordinary fixed offshore wind turbines in most places.\n\nInstead, Portugal has pioneered floating wind: the WindFloat Atlantic farm off Viana do Castelo, opened in 2020, was the first of its kind in continental Europe.

P.title: pt-sea.c9.text
Portugal: Long stretches of Portugal's coast are retreating as beaches and dunes lose sand. Dams hold back sediment that rivers once delivered, and harbour walls block the sand's natural drift.\n\nSea level is rising too, so storms reach further inland. Towns like Espinho and Costa da Caparica spend heavily defending their beaches.

P.title: na-portugal.q0.q
Portugal: What is Portugal's only national park?

P.title: na-portugal.q1.q
Portugal: How often is cork harvested from a tree?

P.title: na-portugal.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal sits in the Mediterranean hotspot, with Atlantic and Mediterranean influences, plus the unique islands of Madeira and the Azores.

P.title: na-portugal.c1.text
Portugal: Portugal's only national park, created in 1971, protects mountains, oak forests, Garrano horses, wolves and golden eagles.

P.title: na-portugal.c2.text
Portugal: Madeira's laurel forest is a relic of forests that covered Southern Europe millions of years ago. It's a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999.

P.title: na-portugal.c3.text
Portugal: The Tagus estuary is one of Europe's most important wetlands for birds, hosting tens of thousands of waders and flamingos in winter.

P.title: na-portugal.c4.text
Portugal: The Sado estuary near Setúbal has a resident population of bottlenose dolphins, one of the few in Europe, numbering around 30.

P.title: na-portugal.c5.text
Portugal: The Berlengas archipelago off Peniche is a nature reserve and UNESCO biosphere reserve, home to seabird colonies and rich marine life.

P.title: na-portugal.c6.text
Portugal: Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, with roughly half of global output. Cork is stripped by hand every nine years without felling the tree.

P.title: na-portugal.c7.text
Portugal: Large eucalyptus and pine plantations, abandonment of farmland and hotter summers have made wildfires a major threat. Native oaks burn less readily.

P.title: na-portugal.c8.text
Portugal: Griffon and black vultures have returned to the Douro International and Tejo International parks, thanks to feeding stations and protection.

P.title: na-portugal.c9.text
Portugal: Gerês for wolves and horses, the Tagus estuary for flamingos, Sado for dolphins, Douro International for vultures and the Azores for whales.

P.title: pt-food.summary
Portugal: Cod, sardines, convent sweets, olive oil, cheese, wine and coffee.

P.title: pt-food.q0.q
Portugal: What sets the milk for Serra da Estrela cheese?

P.title: pt-food.q0.x
Portugal: The cardoon thistle's flowers curdle the ewe's milk.

P.title: pt-food.q1.q
Portugal: What does "verde" mean in Vinho Verde?

P.title: pt-food.q1.x
Portugal: It is a young wine and can be white, red or rosé.

P.title: pt-food.q2.q
Portugal: Where did the White Fleet sail to catch cod?

P.title: pt-food.q2.x
Portugal: Cod lives in cold northern seas.

P.title: pt-food.q3.q
Portugal: Which Japanese dish probably has Portuguese roots?

P.title: pt-food.q3.x
Portugal: Frying in batter arrived with Portuguese traders.

P.title: pt-food.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal and Galicia share what nutritionists call the Atlantic diet: plenty of fish, vegetables, potatoes, bread and olive oil, with a little wine, eaten slowly with family.\n\nIt looks like the Mediterranean diet, but it leans more on the sea, on cabbage and potatoes, and on soups and stews cooked for hours.

P.title: pt-food.c0.viz.items.3
Portugal: Slow stews shared at the table

P.title: pt-food.c1.text
Portugal: Portugal's favourite fish doesn't live in Portuguese waters. Fishermen sailed to Newfoundland and Greenland to catch cod, salting it on board so it would keep for months.\n\nToday most bacalhau comes from Norway and Iceland, but the Portuguese way of salting, drying and soaking it remains a national ritual.

P.title: pt-food.c2.text
Portugal: Grilled sardines are the smell of a Portuguese summer. They are best from about June to October, when they are fat and oily, and are eaten on a slice of bread that soaks up the juices.\n\nPortugal is also famous for tinned fish: canneries have packed sardines, tuna and mackerel in olive oil since the 19th century.

P.title: pt-food.c3.text
Portugal: Portugal is small, but each region cooks differently. The green, rainy north eats hearty soups, tripe and cured meats; the centre roasts suckling pig; the Alentejo makes bread soups and pork dishes; the Algarve cooks fish and shellfish.\n\nThe islands add their own: stews cooked in volcanic ground in the Azores, and beef skewers on bay-wood sticks in Madeira.

P.title: pt-food.c4.text
Portugal: Olive oil, azeite, is the fat of Portuguese cooking. It dresses fish and boiled potatoes, finishes soups and is poured generously over bacalhau.\n\nPortugal has become one of the world's leading producers, mainly thanks to new irrigated groves in the Alentejo. Traditional varieties such as Galega and Cobrançosa give oils from mild to peppery.

P.title: pt-food.c5.text
Portugal: Portugal's best-known cheeses are made from ewe's milk and set not with animal rennet but with the flowers of a wild thistle. The result is often soft, creamy and slightly bitter.\n\nSerra da Estrela is the most famous, but Azeitão, Nisa, Évora and São Jorge from the Azores all have protected status.

P.title: pt-food.c6.text
Portugal: Many Portuguese sweets were born in convents and monasteries. Nuns and monks used egg whites to starch linen and clear wine, leaving mountains of yolks, which they mixed with sugar from Madeira and Brazil.\n\nThe results have heavenly names: toucinho do céu, papos de anjo, barriga de freira. The pastel de nata is the most famous heir of this tradition.

P.title: pt-food.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal packs very different wines into a small country. In the rainy Minho, Vinho Verde is light and fresh. Up the Douro valley, terraced schist slopes give port and powerful reds. On the hot Alentejo plains, wines are ripe and smooth.\n\nMost are made from native grapes found almost nowhere else, such as Alvarinho, Touriga Nacional and Antão Vaz.

P.title: pt-food.c8.text
Portugal: In Portugal, um café means a short, strong espresso, drunk standing at the counter in a minute or two, often several times a day. In Lisbon it's a bica, in Porto a cimbalino.\n\nCafés and pastelarias are neighbourhood living rooms. Coffee is cheap, usually about €1 or less, and roasted in a dark, smooth style shaped by Portugal's links with Brazil and Africa.

P.title: pt-food.c9.text
Portugal: Japanese tempura probably owes its start to Portuguese traders and missionaries, who reached Japan in the 1540s. They fried fish and vegetables in batter, much like Portugal's peixinhos da horta, battered green beans.\n\nThe name may come from têmporas, the Ember Days, when Catholics avoided meat. Portuguese cooking also left its mark in Goa, Macau, Malacca and Brazil.

P.title: pt-fado.summary
Portugal: Fado, cante, the song of 25 April and folk instruments.

P.title: pt-fado.q0.q
Portugal: When was fado added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list?

P.title: pt-fado.q1.q
Portugal: What did "Grândola, Vila Morena" signal on 25 April 1974?

P.title: pt-fado.q1.o1
Portugal: The go-ahead for the military coup

P.title: pt-fado.q1.x
Portugal: Rádio Renascença played it just after midnight.

P.title: pt-fado.q2.q
Portugal: Which instrument became the Hawaiian ukulele?

P.title: pt-fado.q2.x
Portugal: Madeiran workers brought it to Hawaii in 1879.

P.title: pt-fado.q3.x
Portugal: It keeps the chords and the rhythm.

P.title: pt-fado.c0.text
Portugal: Fado is Lisbon's urban song: a single voice, with the Portuguese guitar and a classical guitar, singing of love, jealousy, poverty, the sea and fate. The word comes from the Latin fatum, destiny.\n\nIt grew in the city's poor riverside districts in the 19th century, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible heritage in 2011.

P.title: pt-fado.c0.viz.items.0
Portugal: One voice, often in a black shawl

P.title: pt-fado.c0.viz.items.2
Portugal: Songs of fate, love and loss

P.title: pt-fado.c1.text
Portugal: The classic place to hear fado is a casa de fado, a small restaurant where singers take turns between courses. When the lights dim, waiters stop serving and the room falls silent.\n\nIn fado vadio, "vagrant fado", amateurs stand up to sing in neighbourhood taverns, keeping the tradition alive away from the tourist trail.

P.title: pt-fado.c2.text
Portugal: Fado has two homes. In Lisbon, singers often set new poems to a stock of traditional melodies, such as the fado menor or fado corrido, and phrase them freely.\n\nCoimbra's fado grew in its university: composed songs sung by men at night, tied to student life, farewells and the city itself.

P.title: pt-fado.c3.text
Portugal: In fado, "guitarra" means the pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, while "viola" is the ordinary six-string guitar. The guitarra answers the singer's lines; the viola keeps the harmony and pulse.\n\nThe players follow the singer closely, since melodies stretch and pause. Instrumental pieces called guitarradas let the guitarra shine on its own.

P.title: pt-fado.c4.text
Portugal: Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) took fado from Lisbon's taverns to concert halls across the world. Born into a poor family, she sold fruit on the Lisbon docks as a girl before her voice made her a star.\n\nShe sang great poets, worked with composers who widened fado's sound, and remains the voice most people link with Portugal.

P.title: pt-fado.c5.text
Portugal: Under the dictatorship, fado lyrics had to be approved by censors before being sung in public, and professional singers needed an official licence. Fado moved from the streets into licensed fado houses.\n\nThe regime favoured a tidy, patriotic fado, and after 1974 some saw it as the old regime's music. It took years for fado to lose that label.

P.title: pt-fado.c6.text
Portugal: Cante alentejano, the unaccompanied group singing of the Alentejo, joined UNESCO's list in 2014. Its songs, called modas, are slow and spacious, like the plains they come from.\n\nOnce sung in fields, mines and taverns, cante now lives in choirs, festivals and schools, and young groups mix it with new music.

P.title: pt-fado.c7.text
Portugal: Just after midnight on 25 April 1974, Rádio Renascença played José Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena". It was the second signal for army officers to begin the coup that ended 48 years of dictatorship.\n\nThe song, about brotherhood and equality in an Alentejo town, became the anthem of the Carnation Revolution and is still sung at every 25 April celebration.

P.title: pt-fado.c8.text
Portugal: Beyond fado, Portuguese folk music uses a family of local instruments: the small cavaquinho, regional guitars called violas, bagpipes in the north-east and square drums in the Beira.\n\nEach region has its own sound. Many of these instruments nearly vanished in the 20th century and have been revived by folk groups and young musicians.

P.title: pt-fado.c9.text
Portugal: Portuguese music today mixes old and new. Since the late 1990s, a generation of fadistas has brought fado back to young audiences, often with new instruments and poets.\n\nLisbon is also a hub for sounds from Angola, Cape Verde and Brazil, while pop, rap and folk artists sing in Portuguese with growing confidence.

P.title: pt-fado.c9.viz.items.0
Portugal: New fado: young voices, new poets

P.title: ar-portugal.c0.text
Portugal: The Portuguese guitar has 12 strings in six pairs and a pear-shaped body, giving fado its shimmering sound. Carlos Paredes made it famous as a solo instrument.

P.title: ar-portugal.c1.text
Portugal: Coimbra fado is sung by men, traditionally students in black capes, often as serenades. It's more lyrical and academic than Lisbon fado.

P.title: ar-portugal.c2.text
Portugal: Lisbon's National Azulejo Museum, in the Madre de Deus convent, shows five centuries of tiles, including a 23-metre panorama of Lisbon before the 1755 earthquake.

P.title: ar-portugal.c3.text
Portugal: Portugal's black and white stone pavements are laid by hand by calceteiros. The waves of Rossio square inspired Copacabana's promenade in Rio.

P.title: ar-portugal.c4.text
Portugal: Portuguese filigree, especially from Gondomar and Póvoa de Lanhoso, twists fine gold and silver threads into delicate jewellery, like the heart of Viana.

P.title: ar-portugal.c5.text
Portugal: In June, cities celebrate saints: Santo António in Lisbon with grilled sardines and basil pots, São João in Porto with plastic hammers and leeks.

P.title: ar-portugal.c6.text
Portugal: The Barcelos rooster legend tells of a pilgrim wrongly accused of theft; a roasted rooster crowed to prove his innocence. It became a national symbol.

P.title: ar-portugal.c7.text
Portugal: Fernando Pessoa, Eça de Queirós, Sophia de Mello Breyner and José Saramago are pillars of Portuguese literature.

P.title: ar-portugal.c8.text
Portugal: Alentejo's polyphonic choral singing, without instruments, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2014. Groups of men or women sing slow, deep songs about the land.

P.title: ar-portugal.c9.text
Portugal: Portuguese is spoken by about 260 million people across four continents, the most spoken language in the Southern Hemisphere.

P.title: pt-architecture.summary
Portugal: From Romanesque cathedrals to Manueline, Pombaline and the Porto School.

P.title: pt-architecture.q0.q
Portugal: Which king gives the Manueline style its name?

P.title: pt-architecture.q1.q
Portugal: Whose tombs face each other at Alcobaça?

P.title: pt-architecture.q1.o1
Portugal: Pedro I and Inês de Castro

P.title: pt-architecture.q1.x
Portugal: Tradition says they will see each other first on Judgement Day.

P.title: pt-architecture.q2.x
Portugal: It ties walls and floors so buildings sway instead of collapsing.

P.title: pt-architecture.q3.q
Portugal: Which Portuguese architect won the Pritzker Prize in 2011?

P.title: pt-architecture.c0.text
Portugal: Portugal's oldest great churches are Romanesque, built mostly in the 12th and 13th centuries as the kingdom took shape. They have thick granite walls, round arches and small windows.\n\nCathedrals such as those of Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra look like castles, with battlements, because they were built in a time of war.

P.title: pt-architecture.c1.text
Portugal: King Afonso Henriques gave Alcobaça to Cistercian monks in 1153. Its church, begun in 1178, was one of the first Gothic buildings in Portugal.\n\nIts long, bare, white nave reflects Cistercian ideals of simplicity. Inside lie the carved tombs of King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, Portugal's most famous lovers.

P.title: pt-architecture.c2.text
Portugal: King João I promised a monastery to the Virgin Mary if he won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385. The result, Batalha ("battle"), took over a century to build and is a masterpiece of Portuguese Gothic.\n\nIts chapter house has a vault about 19 metres wide with no central column, and its Unfinished Chapels are open to the sky.

P.title: pt-architecture.c3.text
Portugal: Manueline is Portugal's own late Gothic style, from about 1490 to 1530, the age of King Manuel I. It covers doors, windows and columns with carved ropes, anchors, shells and coral.\n\nIt was paid for by the wealth of the sea route to India, and its decoration celebrates the voyages and the king's power.

P.title: pt-architecture.c3.viz.items.2
Portugal: Cross of the Order of Christ

P.title: pt-architecture.c4.text
Portugal: On the riverbank at Belém stand Portugal's two most famous Manueline buildings. The Jerónimos Monastery, begun in 1501, holds the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões.\n\nThe Belém Tower, built about 1514–1519, guarded the entrance to Lisbon's harbour. Both have been World Heritage Sites since 1983.

P.title: pt-architecture.c5.text
Portugal: Azulejos moved from church interiors onto the outside of houses in the 19th century. Emigrants returning from Brazil, where tiled façades were common, are thought to have brought the fashion home, and factories made patterned tiles cheaply.\n\nTiles protect walls from rain and reflect light. Today whole streets in Lisbon, Porto, Aveiro and Ovar are wrapped in them.

P.title: pt-architecture.c6.text
Portugal: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt with the gaiola pombalina, a timber cage hidden inside masonry walls. Its diagonal braces help a building sway rather than burst apart.\n\nThe same planning ideas created a whole new town, Vila Real de Santo António in the Algarve, laid out from 1774.

P.title: pt-architecture.c7.text
Portugal: The Estado Novo dictatorship (1933–1974) used architecture to project order and national pride. After an early modernist phase, it favoured a "Português Suave" style that dressed modern structures in traditional roofs, arches and stone.\n\nIts legacy includes courthouses, schools, housing estates, the Padrão dos Descobrimentos and the bridge over the Tagus, now called 25 de Abril.

P.title: pt-architecture.c8.text
Portugal: Álvaro Siza (born 1933) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (born 1952) both won the Pritzker Prize, in 1992 and 2011. Both came from the "Porto School", shaped by Fernando Távora.\n\nTheir buildings are calm, precise and shaped by their sites: pools set among sea rocks, a stadium cut into a quarry, white walls that frame the light.

P.title: pt-architecture.c9.text
Portugal: Portuguese pavement is still laid by hand, stone by stone, by craftsmen called calceteiros. White limestone and black basalt are cut into small cubes and set in sand to make waves, stars and ships.\n\nIn 2021 the craft was added to Portugal's national inventory of intangible heritage. But it is slippery when wet, and cities debate where to keep it.

P.title: pt-science.summary
Portugal: From navigators' instruments to modern labs: Portugal's scientists and what they discovered.

P.title: pt-science.q0.q
Portugal: What did Pedro Nunes' nonius help navigators and astronomers do?

P.title: pt-science.q0.x
Portugal: It inspired the vernier scale on callipers.

P.title: pt-science.q1.q
Portugal: Who showed King João V a small hot-air balloon in 1709?

P.title: pt-science.q1.x
Portugal: It rose 74 years before the Montgolfiers' public flight.

P.title: pt-science.q2.q
Portugal: What did Egas Moniz win the 1949 Nobel Prize for?

P.title: pt-science.q2.x
Portugal: The operation was later abandoned, and the prize is still debated.

P.title: pt-science.q3.q
Portugal: Which agency, created in 1996, runs Portugal's network of science centres?

P.title: pt-science.q3.x
Portugal: Its flagship is Lisbon's Pavilhão do Conhecimento.

P.title: pt-science.c0.text
Portugal: Out of sight of land, 15th-century Portuguese pilots needed to know how far north or south they were. They found latitude by measuring the height of the Pole Star or the noon Sun.\n\nSimple instruments, printed rules and astronomical tables turned this into a routine that ordinary pilots could learn.

P.title: pt-science.c1.text
Portugal: In 1542 the mathematician Pedro Nunes proposed a clever way to read angles more finely than the marks on an instrument allowed.\n\nHis idea, the nonius, used many concentric scales. Simplified a century later, it lives on in the vernier scale of every calliper.

P.title: pt-science.c2.text
Portugal: Garcia de Orta was a Portuguese physician who lived in Goa for over 30 years. In 1563 he published the Colóquios, a book on the medicinal plants and drugs of Asia.\n\nWritten as lively dialogues, it tested old claims against what he saw, tasted and learnt from local healers.

P.title: pt-science.c3.text
Portugal: In August 1709 Bartolomeu de Gusmão, a priest born in Brazil, showed King João V a small paper balloon lifted by hot air, indoors in Lisbon.\n\nHe also designed a bird-shaped airship, the Passarola. It almost certainly never flew, but it made him famous as "the Flying Priest".

P.title: pt-science.c4.text
Portugal: Egas Moniz, neurologist and politician, won Portugal's first Nobel Prize in 1949 for the leucotomy, a brain operation for severe mental illness.\n\nThe operation was later abandoned, and his prize is still debated. His story is now used to teach how medicine should test new treatments.

P.title: pt-science.c5.text
Portugal: Abel Salazar (1889–1946) was a Porto doctor and researcher who studied tissues under the microscope and invented a staining method.\n\nHe was also a painter and writer. In 1935 the dictatorship removed him from his university post for his ideas. He was no relation of the dictator Salazar.

P.title: pt-science.c6.text
Portugal: Under the dictatorship, few Portuguese did research. After democracy returned in 1974, and especially from the 1990s, Portugal invested heavily in science.\n\nSpending on research more than tripled as a share of the economy, and thousands of young people were funded to earn doctorates at home and abroad.

P.title: pt-science.c7.text
Portugal: Ciência Viva, created in 1996, is Portugal's agency for spreading scientific culture. It runs a network of about 20 science centres, from Bragança to the Algarve and the islands.\n\nIts flagship is the Pavilhão do Conhecimento in Lisbon, a hands-on science museum in a building from Expo '98.

P.title: pt-science.c8.text
Portugal: When industrialist António Champalimaud died in 2004, he left about a quarter of his fortune, around €500 million, to create a foundation for medical research.\n\nIts Champalimaud Centre for the Unknown, opened in 2010 on the Tagus at Belém, studies the brain and cancer and treats patients.

P.title: pt-science.c9.text
Portugal: Portuguese scientists today work in fields from neuroscience and cancer to ocean science, materials and space. Many institutes host international teams.\n\nPortugal is a member of CERN, the European Space Agency and the European Southern Observatory, and its researchers win competitive European grants.

P.title: pt-traditions.summary
Portugal: Carnival, Easter, the June saints, romarias, Christmas and saudade.

P.title: pt-traditions.q0.x
Portugal: It's eaten on the night of 24 December.

P.title: pt-traditions.q1.q
Portugal: Which carnival was added to UNESCO's list in 2019?

P.title: pt-traditions.q1.x
Portugal: Its masked caretos wear bright woollen fringes.

P.title: pt-traditions.q2.q
Portugal: What do people eat at a magusto?

P.title: pt-traditions.q2.x
Portugal: It's held around São Martinho, 11 November.

P.title: pt-traditions.q3.q
Portugal: Whose feast on 29 June closes the June saints?

P.title: pt-traditions.q3.x
Portugal: As a fisherman, he is loved in coastal towns.

P.title: pt-traditions.c0.text
Portugal: Before Lent comes Carnaval, or Entrudo. Towns hold parades, children dress up, and Shrove Tuesday is often a day off, though not an official holiday.\n\nOld rural customs survive alongside Brazilian-style samba. In Podence, in Trás-os-Montes, masked caretos in bright woollen fringes run through the village shaking cowbells.

P.title: pt-traditions.c1.text
Portugal: Easter is a major family feast in Portugal, especially in the north. In Braga, Holy Week brings solemn night processions that draw thousands of visitors.\n\nOn Easter Sunday, many villages receive the compasso, a small procession that visits homes with a cross. Godparents give their godchildren folar, a sweet or savoury Easter bread.

P.title: pt-traditions.c1.viz.items.0
Portugal: Lent: fish, not meat, on Fridays

P.title: pt-traditions.c2.text
Portugal: Lisbon's favourite saint is Santo António. On the night of 12 June every old neighbourhood becomes an arraial, a street party with grilled sardines, bifanas, beer and music.\n\nThe saint is known as a matchmaker and a finder of lost things, and each year the city hosts weddings in his name.

P.title: pt-traditions.c3.text
Portugal: São João is Porto's biggest night. On 23 June the city stays out until dawn, tapping strangers on the head with plastic hammers, waving leeks, grilling sardines and eating caldo verde.\n\nAt midnight, fireworks burst over the Douro. Many people then walk to the sea at Foz to wait for sunrise. Braga also holds a huge São João.

P.title: pt-traditions.c4.text
Portugal: São Pedro, on 29 June, closes the month of the popular saints. As Saint Peter was a fisherman, his feast is strongest in coastal towns.\n\nIn Póvoa de Varzim, neighbourhoods compete with decorated streets, cascatas and rusgas, groups of singers and dancers in fishermen's dress. Sintra, Montijo and Évora also hold big São Pedro fairs.

P.title: pt-traditions.c5.text
Portugal: A romaria is a festival built around a pilgrimage to a chapel or shrine. It mixes a religious procession with a fair: brass bands, drums, folk dancing, stalls of sweets and fireworks.\n\nSummer is romaria season, above all in the north. Viana do Castelo's Senhora d'Agonia in August is one of the biggest, with streets carpeted in coloured sawdust and flowers.

P.title: pt-traditions.c6.text
Portugal: On 1 November, All Saints' Day, children in many places go door to door asking for "pão por Deus", bread for God's sake, and receive bread, nuts, apples and sweets.\n\nOn 11 November, São Martinho, families gather for a magusto: chestnuts roasted over a fire, with young wine. A spell of mild weather around then is called the "summer of São Martinho".

P.title: pt-traditions.c7.text
Portugal: Portugal's main Christmas meal is the consoada, on the night of 24 December. The classic menu is boiled bacalhau with cabbage, potatoes and eggs, all drizzled with olive oil and garlic.\n\nThen come sweets like rabanadas, sonhos and filhoses, and many families open presents at midnight. Bolo-rei, a ring-shaped fruit cake, stays on the table until 6 January.

P.title: pt-traditions.c8.text
Portugal: The colourful clay rooster is Portugal's best-known souvenir, but it comes from a real craft tradition. Barcelos, in the Minho, has made pottery for centuries from the clay of the Cávado valley.\n\nBesides roosters, its potters model whole worlds in clay, called figurado: musicians, devils, animals and village scenes, often full of humour and fantasy.

P.title: pt-traditions.c9.text
Portugal: Saudade is a longing for someone or something absent: a person, a place, a time, even something that may never return. It can feel sad and sweet at once.\n\nThe Portuguese often call it untranslatable and see it as part of the national character. It runs through fado, poetry and everyday speech: "tenho saudades tuas" means "I miss you".

P.title: pt-sport.summary
Portugal: Football legends, world-beating roller hockey, giant waves, marathon heroes, cycling and sailing.

Portugal: Who scored four goals against North Korea at the 1966 World Cup?

P.title: pt-sport.q0.x
Portugal: Portugal came back from 3–0 down to win 5–3.

Portugal: Who scored the winning goal in the Euro 2016 final?

P.title: pt-sport.q1.x
Portugal: His low shot in extra time beat France 1–0.

P.title: pt-sport.q2.q
Portugal: Which athlete won Portugal's first Olympic gold?

P.title: pt-sport.q2.x
Portugal: Lopes won the marathon in Los Angeles in 1984, aged 37.

P.title: pt-sport.q3.q
Portugal: Why does Nazaré get such huge waves?

P.title: pt-sport.q3.o1
Portugal: An undersea canyon focuses the swell

P.title: pt-sport.q3.x
Portugal: The Nazaré Canyon channels the energy of Atlantic storms.

P.title: pt-sport.c0.text
Portugal: Football is Portugal's most popular sport. Three clubs, Benfica, FC Porto and Sporting, have won almost every league title since the league began in the 1930s.\n\nOnly two other clubs have ever been champions: Belenenses in 1946 and Boavista in 2001. Each of the big three has millions of supporters at home and abroad.

P.title: pt-sport.c1.text
Portugal: Eusébio da Silva Ferreira, born in Mozambique in 1942, became one of the greatest strikers in history with Benfica and Portugal.\n\nNicknamed the Black Panther, he won the Ballon d'Or in 1965 and was top scorer at the 1966 World Cup, where Portugal finished third.

P.title: pt-sport.c2.text
Portugal: Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Funchal, Madeira, in 1985, is one of the most successful footballers ever. He has won five Ballon d'Or awards and five Champions League titles.\n\nHe is the top scorer and most capped player in men's international football, and captained Portugal to its first trophies.

P.title: pt-sport.c3.text
Portugal: For decades Portugal's national team played attractive football but won nothing. That changed at Euro 2016 in France, when Portugal beat the hosts 1–0 in the final.\n\nThey added the first UEFA Nations League in 2019, at home in Porto, and won it again in 2025, beating Spain on penalties in Munich.

P.title: pt-sport.c4.text
Portugal: Roller hockey, or hóquei em patins, is played on four-wheeled roller skates with a stick and a hard ball. Portugal is one of the sport's great powers.\n\nIts men's team has won the world championship more than 15 times, rivalled mainly by Spain, Argentina and Italy.

P.title: pt-sport.c5.text
Portugal: In winter, Praia do Norte in Nazaré produces some of the biggest surfable waves on Earth. An undersea canyon focuses the energy of Atlantic storms.\n\nSurfers towed in by jet-ski have ridden waves of over 25 metres there. Portugal's whole coast, from Peniche to Ericeira, is a surfing destination.

P.title: pt-sport.c5.viz.steps.2
Portugal: Waves rise at Praia do Norte

P.title: pt-sport.c6.text
Portugal: Portugal's first Olympic gold medal came in the marathon: Carlos Lopes won in Los Angeles in 1984, aged 37.\n\nFour years later Rosa Mota won the women's marathon in Seoul, becoming Portugal's first female Olympic champion. Together they made distance running a national passion.

P.title: pt-sport.c7.text
Portugal: After the marathon golds, Fernanda Ribeiro won the 10,000 m in Atlanta in 1996 with a fierce final lap.\n\nNelson Évora and Pedro Pichardo later won the triple jump, and in Paris 2024 Iúri Leitão and Rui Oliveira took gold in track cycling. Portugal has won six Olympic golds in all.

P.title: pt-sport.c8.text
Portugal: The Volta a Portugal, first held in 1927, is the country's great cycling stage race. Each summer it crosses the country for about ten days, with crowds lining the mountain climbs.\n\nPortuguese riders have also shone abroad, from Joaquim Agostinho in the Tour de France to world champion Rui Costa and João Almeida.

P.title: pt-sport.c9.text
Portugal: With a long Atlantic coast and a seafaring past, Portugal has a strong sailing tradition. Portuguese sailors won Olympic silver in 1948 and bronze in 1996.\n\nLisbon and Cascais regularly host major regattas, and the steady summer north wind makes the coast a favourite for windsurfing and kitesurfing.
